items.title: LuthorSQL: A One-Pass Text-to-SQL Model as System 1 for a Slower LLM Agent
items.summary: Frontier LLM agents that query databases with tools are among the most accurate text-to-SQL systems, but per-query calls to a hosted model are slow, costly, and expose sensitive organizational queries to external APIs. For example, a Claude Opus 5.5 agent serving 10,000 queries a day costs over $70,000 a year at list price. To what extent can local hardware already owned by an organization offload this burden without compromising the agent's accuracy? We present LuthorSQL, a non-autoregressive 7B text-to-SQL model that serves as a rapid System 1 gate for a slower LLM agent (System 2), escalating queries only when uncertain. LuthorSQL makes a single forward pass to predict slot scores over a bounded grammar for query plans, compiles and runs up to 32 candidate plans, and chooses an answer using a trained validator. On its own, LuthorSQL reaches 68.03% execution accuracy on BIRD's hidden test set at 0.84 s per question on a single GPU, maintains its accuracy in 9 GB with 8-bit quantized weights, and transfers zero-shot to Snowflake, BigQuery, MySQL, PostgreSQL, and DuckDB within 3.1 points of its native SQLite accuracy. Combined with Claude Opus 5.5 in a pre-registered confidence cascade over 227 questions on databases published after Opus's training cutoff, LuthorSQL answers nearly half of all questions locally and cuts API cost by 33.3% at the same accuracy. Finally, contamination probing shows that Opus reproduces 48-92% of public benchmark gold queries verbatim without seeing the schema; however, its tool-assisted accuracy holds on renamed schemas and reaches 95.6-97.4% on post-cutoff databases. Code and data: https://github.com/IAMIbrahimmemon/luthorsql

items.title: WeightBench: Evaluating Language Models as Weight-Space Programmers
items.summary: Recent work shows that large language models (LLMs) can operate directly on the parameters of other neural networks. They can read what a network was trained to do, fix a network that fails, and write working networks from scratch, all without gradient descent. This capability has been termed Weight-Space Programming (WSP). Exploring this new paradigm systematically requires a robust benchmark. We introduce WEIGHTBENCH, a benchmark that evaluates LLMs of increasing capability on 42 WSP tasks across five tracks: reading, fixing and writing weights, recognizing edits that are impossible, and data-free compression. The networks whose weights the LLMs read and edit range from 2K-parameter control policies to 7B-parameter language models. Experimental benchmark results show that frontier agents can already read small networks and write working control policies without ever running them, but cannot yet patch language models, compress them without data, or tell an impossible edit from a hard one. On all 42 tasks, Claude Opus 5.5 reaches a macro score of 0.535 (Sonnet 5.5 0.466, Haiku 5.5 0.402, DeepSeek v4-flash 0.215); on the 38 tasks it was run on, GPT-6.1-sol reaches 0.568 against Opus's 0.546. Code, the task registry, our OS-level sandbox harness, and the live leaderboard are publicly available at https://github.com/Aayush-Marasini/WeightBench.

items.title: VelServe: Taming Decode Jitters in LLM Inference with Tail-Calibrated Scheduling
items.summary:
Interactive LLM services must meet latency service-level objectives (SLOs) for the time to first token (TTFT) and the time between tokens (TBT), as streaming and soft real-time applications require predictable token delivery. We identify decode jitters in both aggregated and disaggregated serving. A jitter delays every request in the batch, and long responses span hundreds of steps, so even rare overruns cause many SLO violations. In aggregated serving, SLO-aware schedulers set each step's prefill budget until its predicted latency just meets the TBT target, leaving no room for mispredictions or host stalls. Disaggregation meets average TBT targets at a cost in capacity, yet the steps that admit new requests still run late.
  We present \sysname, a scheduler that calibrates how much prefill work each decode step carries using the measured tail of its own iteration latency. The SLO determines how rare a late step must be, and \sysname leaves enough headroom in each iteration to prevent overruns and meet the target decode latency. This headroom slows prefill, so \sysname serves the shortest waiting prompt first. When TTFT deadlines grow with prompt length, the long prompts it delays have the most time to spare. Under disaggregation, it spaces admissions so that no request waits on more slow admission steps than its P99 target allows. On three attention families and varying workloads, \sysname sustains 2.4--2.9$\times$ the SLO goodput of the strongest baseline on Qwen3-8B and DeepSeek-V4-Flash, and at least 4.4$\times$ on DeepSeek-V2-Lite. With prefill and decode disaggregated on eight GPUs, \sysname meets the SLO for more than twice as many requests as state-of-the-art baselines.

items.story_key: model:gemini|ver:4|title:introducing gemini 4 hydrogen
items.content_excerpt: Today, we’re introducing Gemini 4 Hydrogen, bringing cutting-edge intelligence to everyone — with speed and efficiency for everyday coding and agentic workflows. While our frontier models, Gemini 4 Carbon and Gemini 4 Argon , excel at deep, long-horizon reasoning on your hardest problems, Hydrogen is built for rapid execution across diverse agentic workflows. With Hydrogen, we’re also bringing Gemini 4 to everyone — for all tiers of Google AI Studio , the Gemini API, Gemini for business , the Gemini app , Google Search , and paid Google AI Pro and Ultra subscribers in Google Antigravity . Hydrogen surpasses Argon on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index at its default high thinking level (51 vs. 50, and reaching 54 at its highest xhigh thinking setting), while often completing tasks faster than models in its class. Gemini 4 Hydrogen is priced flat across its entire 1 million-token context window at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens. In real-world software development, while teams rely on frontier models like Carbon and Argon for deep architectural judgment when designing systems or untangling subtle bugs, they still need a fast, disciplined execution model for writing code, running tests, and verifying changes. Hydrogen is built to stand on its own as a model for everyday work — or to pair with Carbon and Argon as the high-efficiency execution engine in multi-model workflows. To help make this multi-model collaboration automatic, we’re introducing Orchestrator in Google Antigravity . Rather than using a single model from start to finish, Orchestrator dynamically switches between models like Carbon and Hydrogen within the same session. On Terminal-Bench 4.0 , Orchestrator reached near-Carbon task success rates while, on average, consuming 24% less quota and completing 19% faster. For workflows that require parallel agents, Carbon can act as the coordinator while Hydrogen can power worker and verifier agents to build and test changes simultaneously across isolated workspaces — helping teams ship complex projects faster without driving up token costs. Beyond multi-model workflows, Hydrogen is a major standalone upgrade for teams migrating from Gemini 3.8 Flash. items.title: Which Claude model should you build with? Fable, Opus, Sonnet, or Haiku
items.summary: Which Claude model to pick, what they cost, and how to use them together.
items.story_key: model:claude|title:which claude model should you build with fable opus sonnet or haiku
items.content_excerpt: The current Claude lineup has four generally available models: Claude Haiku 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5, Claude Opus 5.5 and Claude Fable 5.2. Claude Mythos 5.2 is our most capable model for cybersecurity and life sciences research, available through our verification programs. If you build on the Claude Platform or work in Claude Code , you may be wondering which model to use for your common tasks. This article will help answer that question and how to think about the trade-offs. The quick answer is that you should start most work on Opus 5.5 at its default effort level, medium . There's a reason it's the default model in Claude Code. It costs half as much per input and output token as Fable 5.2, and it's the model we recommend starting with for most coding and knowledge work. Before you move models, try adjusting your effort level. It's a finer dial for both cost and capability. Past high , one more effort level can cost as much as a bigger model, so compare both on your own work. If you're past high , test the next model up at a lower effort instead. Conversely, one level down can get you the result you need at a lower rate. Higher effort helps when the model needs to think longer, call more tools, or check its own work more. Just keep in mind that it also adds latency. Additionally, moving to a higher effort level won't give a model knowledge or skill it doesn't have. For that, you still need to move up a model. Prices are Claude API list prices. For benchmark results, see the Fable 5.2 page . When you choose between models, you're making a trade-off. When you pick a larger model, for example, you are choosing capability over latency. These are the main trade-offs to think through. Generally, bigger models cost more per token and are more capable, but the cost vs capability trade-off isn't universally true at the task level. A higher price per token doesn't always mean a higher cost per task, or a better result. As we showed in Spending your effort , on Anthropic's runs of Terminal-Bench 3.0, the previous Fable, 5.1, at max scored 58.0%, while Opus 5.5 at high scored 58.9% with half the tokens. On the hardest work, the price gap can close. On FrontierCode 2.0, Fable 5.2 at high scored about level with Opus 5.5 at max (45.3% vs. 45.5%) for roughly half the cost per task. items.title: Inkling 2 Small on vLLM: Day-0 Support
items.summary: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small from day 0: attention residuals, a new decode kernel for relative-bias attention, all-reduce fused with the ops around it, and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|variant:small|title:inkling 2 small on vllm day 0 support
items.content_excerpt: vLLM supports Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Small on day 0. It is a multimodal (text and vision) MoE model with 594B total and 17B active parameters and up to 1M tokens of context. The model also comes with a native DSpark speculator. vLLM supports it with optimized performance (up to 630 TPS/user at TP4 and acceptance length 3.5) and also supports LoRA. Figure 1. Inkling 2 Small architecture. Gold marks what is new or changed since Inkling. Inkling backbone + recent advances. Inkling 2 Small keeps Inkling's backbone: the 5:1 mix of sliding-window and full attention, GQA with a learned relative bias instead of RoPE, the four short convolutions per layer and a sigmoid-routed MoE. On top of it, it adds recent advances. Block attention residuals replace the residual stream, so before each sublayer a learned query mixes the outputs of earlier 6-layer blocks. Gated attention puts a sigmoid gate on each head's output, together with a per-token attention sink . It replaces the hMLP image encoder with a 23-layer ViT. Mixed-precision MoE with Four-Over-Six NVFP4. Out of Inkling 2 Small's 48 layers, the experts of the first 40 use NVFP4 and those of the last 8 use MXFP8. The NVFP4 activations use a per-token global scale plus dual-candidate block scales ( Four Over Six ): for each 16-element block, the quantizer tries scaling the block's maximum to 6 and to 4, and keeps whichever gives the lower reconstruction error (MAE). DSpark speculator with an RNN head. The checkpoint also ships a DSpark draft in place of Inkling's 8 chained MTP heads. The speculator has 5 layers and drafts 7 tokens per step. The head is the RNN variant that DeepSeek's DSpark paper described. Kernel fusion and PDL. vLLM aggressively fuses the collective communication and memory-bound ops between sublayers into a single kernel. With attention residuals, each boundary needs an all-reduce, a short convolution, a residual update, the attention-residual mix and an RMSNorm: five memory-bound steps on the same hidden states. The fused kernel, allreduce_conv_mix (gold in Figure 2), runs the all-reduce over NVLink multicast and keeps everything after it in registers. The GEMM, attention, routing and activation kernels launch with programmatic dependent launch (PDL), so each one's prologue overlaps the tail of the previous kernel, which matters at small batch sizes, where a decode step is a long chain of short kernels. items.title: More Agents, More Samples, or More Thinking? Untangling Coordination, Ensembling, and Test-Time Compute in Multi-Agent LLMs
items.summary: Evaluations of multi-agent language models often compare communicating architectures against a single greedy pass. This practice confounds coordination with sample multiplicity and inference compute. We synthesize nine primary empirical evaluations comprising 516 unique multi-agent configurations organized along a resource vector R with six dimensions and a baseline ladder with four categories. Against baselines with a single pass (Category A), multi-agent accuracy differences are negative overall and near zero when omitting the largest contributing study. When evaluated against baselines matched on sample count (Category B) or resource budget (Category C), multi-agent systems average -0.042 in accuracy, and multilevel random effects modeling on the log odds scale remains negative across sensitivity checks. Multi-agent accuracy equals or falls below the baseline in 74% of these comparable contrasts, and study means are nonpositive in almost all evaluated studies. Across studies reporting both baselines, moving from a greedy pass to a sampled baseline shifts accuracy differences by -0.038 on average. Because communication adds no information when agents share identical evidence, positive returns require partitioned evidence, external verification, or error diversity across models. We provide a reviewer checklist and accounting utilities.

items.title: Safety Side Effects of Preventative Persona Steering: An Empirical Audit
items.summary: High-level behaviors such as sycophancy and hallucination correspond to directions in a model's activation space (Chen et al., 2025). These directions, known as persona vectors, can suppress undesirable traits either at inference time, subtracting the vector during generation, or through preventative steering, adding the vector during fine-tuning, so the optimizer never needs to encode the trait in weights, then removing the vector at evaluation. Chen et al. (2025) recommend preventative steering because it preserves Massive Multitask Language Understanding (MMLU) accuracy, but validations of this recommendation have measured capability alone. We primarily evaluate results on preventative steering of sycophancy and hallucination vectors on three models, measuring three safety benchmarks alongside trait expression, coherence, and MMLU. Our findings show that preventative steering still changes refusal behavior, but by an amount that depends on the trait and does not establish that preventative persona steering is safety-neutral, and steering methods should be evaluated on several safety benchmarks.

items.title: Encoder Disaggregation in vLLM: Scaling Multimodal Serving with EPD
items.summary: Recent advances in vLLM encoder disaggregation: metadata-only multimodal requests, dedicated encoder execution, remote embedding transfer, cross-encoder caching, and lower-overhead EPD routing.
items.story_key: model:vllm|title:encoder disaggregation in vllm scaling multimodal serving with epd
items.content_excerpt: Multimodal inference adds an encoding stage before language-model execution. Images, video frames, and audio must be processed into embeddings before the language model can use them. The demand on this stage varies with media size, modality, and request mix, and can change independently of prefill and decode demand. Encoder / Prefill / Decode (EPD) disaggregation separates these stages into independently deployed vLLM instances. Recent work in the vLLM community has expanded EPD across model execution, remote embedding transfer, shared caching, multimodal input handling, and request routing. DeepSeek's inference deployment Q&A describes an E/P/D architecture with a separately deployed vision encoder. vLLM has supported encoder disaggregation since our December 2025 architecture post , and continues to improve that support. vLLM main now also supports metadata-only EPD for DeepSeek V4.1 Flash. This post explains the engineering behind that progress, with a focus on five changes: The EPD tracker links the ongoing work. The core vLLM capabilities described below, including MiMo and XPU support, are included in vLLM v0.32.0. DeepSeek V4.1 Flash metadata-only support is available on main through #62802 . The vLLM Router and SMG integrations below use their respective main branches. EPD supports two deployment patterns: E+PD , with a separate encoder and a combined prefill/decode instance, and E/P/D , with all three stages deployed separately. Figure 1. E+PD separates encoding from language-model execution. E/P/D additionally separates prefill and decode. EC connectors deliver encoder embeddings; KV connectors transfer the state between prefill and decode. An image-heavy workload may need more encoder capacity without a corresponding increase in decode capacity. A workload with longer responses may require the opposite. Separating the stages allows operators to adjust their instance counts and execution settings independently, while moving encoder computation off the GPUs serving the language model. Transferring embeddings solves only part of the handoff. The consumer also needs enough information to reconstruct the multimodal input layout: placeholder lengths, image grids, feature lengths, and identifiers linking those positions to the transferred embeddings. A straightforward EPD implementation sends the original media to the encoder, transfers the resulting embeddings through an EC connector, and forwards the original request to P/PD. items.title: claude-code v2.1.323
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added Code Mode, an experimental opt-in in which Claude writes JavaScript to call its tools; see https://code.claude.com/docs/en/code-mode to turn it on, or to turn it off for an organization
  • Added engines["claude-code"] to plugin.json: plugins outside their stated Claude Code version range are not installed, updated or loaded, and install and update pick the newest version that fits
  • Added type checking of a plugin's TypeScript hooks module to claude plugin validate; each finding is a warning, and --strict fails on it
  • Added to claude plugin validate the $ nouns a mod's engine.create hook adds, withholds or replaces
  • Added support for CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_MODEL in managed settings for Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Added an options menu (stop, switch to usage credits, upgrade) when a model needs usage credits that are turned off or used up
  • Added a progress heartbeat every 30 seconds while hooks run long in claude -p and SDK sessions, so a host such as Claude Desktop won't end the turn as hung (once it includes this version)
  • Added .docx support to Artifact tool asset uploads
  • Added a /diff to close hint to the diff panel, and the keys that focus and close a panel to the ? shortcut guide
  • Added a start-up warning for Bash allow rules with a * in a variable's value, such as Bash(PORT=* npm run dev)
  • Added a warning when a plugin's language server can't start, naming the server and what to check
  • Added a one-time startup notice naming CLAUDE_CODE_PERFORCE_MODE when Perforce settings are found and the mode is off
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AGENT_PROGRESS_SUMMARIES (available since 2.1.318): set it to 1 to turn off subagent progress summaries and the requests that write them (#86879)
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_HINT_COMMAND, which a program that starts Claude Code can set to have the exit hint name its own resume command
  • Added unsetOptionCount to the claude plugin install --json result: how many userConfig options are not yet set
  • Added isPromptCovered to the props a mod's pane is drawn with, telling it when a dialog or a field above the prompt covers the prompt
  • Fixed running /compact again, or after a command such as /context, summarizing away a message that Claude had not answered yet
  • Fixed a resumed session joining your next message to an old interrupted message that was not resumed
  • Fixed a memory spike at the next prompt after Claude changed a very large file
  • Fixed a setting saved in a running session undoing a hand edit made to settings.json moments earlier; a settings file you delete during a session now stays deleted
  • Fixed claude plugin commands and claude mcp list signing you out of a Console profile when they ended while the token was being renewed
  • Fixed Edit and Bash running out of memory on certain /proc files, and Edit hanging or running out of memory on devices and named pipes
  • Fixed Claude Code failing to start, or to clear stored credentials at sign-out, when saving its configuration file failed with "Out of memory"
  • Fixed requests sent without streaming failing on errors that streamed requests recover from, such as a rejected image, thinking block or beta header
  • Fixed ExitWorktree, the worktree exit dialog and /resume leaving the session in the wrong folder when the folder the shell was in before entering the worktree had been deleted
  • Fixed accents and other combining marks sometimes landing left of the text, leaving stale copies on screen, or silently disappearing when text wraps
  • Fixed the last key of a key chord, such as Enter in ctrl+x enter, acting on a dialog's text field when the chord's own action isn't available there
  • Fixed ps processes piling up when the process listing Claude Code runs before stopping a command takes too long
  • Fixed subagent transcripts and large tool results being saved apart from the session's transcript after entering a worktree created by a WorktreeCreate hook or belonging to a nested repository
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile moving to another sign-in when /fork, the Left arrow or --bg continued it in the background; reopen any session that was open during the update
  • Fixed a background session sending a conversation under another sign-in when its named Anthropic profile is missing, changed or overridden; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed a session on an API key, auth token or workload identity from its shell (not a setup token) moving to another sign-in in the background; it now stops and says so
  • Fixed MCP tool calls ending in the sign-in server's error, such as TOKEN_EXPIRED, instead of asking you to sign in again
  • Fixed an expired claude.ai login showing "Credit balance too low" when a saved Console key or ant auth login profile without credit was used instead
  • Fixed a session on a named Anthropic profile being handed to an older background service that could not keep its sign-in; it now says to restart the service
  • Fixed a background session's sign-in leaving the previous account's login or other credentials in place; it now clears them for every session on the computer, and a refused sign-in can leave no login
  • Fixed background sessions moving between a profile and the stored login when an update restarted them
  • Fixed sessions opened before a sign-in keeping signed-out feature flags after the sign-in
  • Fixed sessions that kept failing after a Claude apps gateway sign-in expired: once you sign in again with /login in another terminal, they carry on at the next message
  • Fixed the billing notice naming your ant auth login organization when a custom X-Api-Key header is set
  • macOS: Fixed "Not logged in · Please run /login" coming back right after a successful /login or a token refresh when the keychain was slow to answer
  • Fixed turns failing in Claude Desktop when an organization's gateway answers an expired token with 403: Claude Code now asks Desktop for a fresh token and retries
  • Fixed the error shown when Amazon Bedrock refuses your account a model: it no longer says to refresh your AWS credentials, it says to enable the model
  • Fixed the awsAuthRefresh or gcpAuthRefresh command sometimes running twice for one request when three or more sessions needed a fresh sign-in at once
  • Fixed the claude -p warning about an ended claude.ai login to say that claude auth logout also removes saved MCP server logins and plugin secrets
  • Fixed Bash permission prompts offering "don't ask again" for commands that write to sensitive paths such as .git or .claude, where the saved rule did not stop the next prompt
  • Fixed a case where some lsof commands ran without a permission prompt
  • Fixed Bash commands that write a file with cat > file <<EOF being shown as "Read 1 file"

items.title: Kitesurf is now open source
items.summary: Kitesurf, our experimental browser engine for AI agents, is now open source. Inspect the code, run it locally, or deploy your own instance on Cloudflare Workers.
items.story_key: story|title:kitesurf is now open source
items.content_excerpt: We introduced Kitesurf , our stateless browser for AI agents that runs entirely on top of Workers, in August and followed up in September with WebMCP support, new APIs, and improved compatibility. On every occasion, we mentioned our commitment to open sourcing it so that developers could run their own browser engine on their own Cloudflare accounts if they want to. That promise is now real. Kitesurf is open source on GitHub under the Apache 2.0 license. You can read the code, run it locally, change it, and deploy your own instance to Cloudflare Workers. Kitesurf runs entirely on Cloudflare Workers. It parses HTML, applies CSS, executes page JavaScript, and renders screenshots without a browser container. It supports the Chrome DevTools Protocol (CDP), so you can connect clients such as Puppeteer. Our main goal is to give AI agents a lightweight, efficient browser — one that can load websites, execute JavaScript, and interact with pages while using less CPU and memory than a full browser like Chromium, and scaling on demand across Cloudflare’s global Workers network. Read more about why and how we built Kitesurf in our initial announcement and how to use it in Browser Run’s developer documentation. Kitesurf builds on Cloudflare’s Developer Platform and APIs, alongside an ecosystem of open-source Rust packages compiled to WebAssembly: These projects made Kitesurf possible. They retain their respective licenses; the repository's NOTICE documents third-party notices. Kitesurf has three main parts: the Engine manages browser sessions and client connections, PageScript runs the page and its JavaScript, and PageRenderer draws the result. All packages, the engine, its Rust core, DOM shims, renderer, and Kitesurf CLI live separately in folders under the repository’s packages directory where you can explore how all the pieces fit together. To run Kitesurf locally, follow the repository's build requirements , then clone the repository , install dependencies, and start the engine: The first build compiles the Rust core and its dependencies, so give it some time. Subsequent builds reuse the build cache. Finally wrangler starts a local development server at http://127.0.0.1:8787 . Open that address to try a page in Chrome DevTools, or use it programmatically. Or you can point your AI harness at the local CDP port (agents love CDP) and watch it take full control of Kitesurf.
